segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Looking at the past tenses, the line in the past and the dot in the past, the line in the past is extremely regular.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We only have a few odd irregular verbs for the line in the past.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Ser is one of them, and we can remember by thinking of an era. So what is the base for ser as a line in the past?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Era, good. So this means I was, you formal were, he, she, it was as a line in the past. How would you say we were?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Éramos, good. The accent doesn't move. Éramos. They were or you guys were?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We had the line in the past of ir, which was a little bit like a mix between the -aba ending that we have for -ar verbs for the line in the past and the -ía ending that we have for -er/-ir verbs in the line in the past. So what was I was going from ir?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. Iba. We were going?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Iban, good. And then we had ver to see. How is I see in the present?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Veo. And this extra e that it keeps for the I form in the present, veo, carries over into the line in the past. So I was seeing, you formal were seeing, he, she, it was seeing is veía.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So the line in the past is a very safe tense. We just have a few irregular verbs, but for the rest we can be very certain that taking off the -ar and putting -aba or taking off the -er/-ir and putting -ía is going to give us the result that we want.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The point in the past is less regular, less reliable. There are a group of verbs in the dot or the point in the past which are irregular, but they all do something very similar. Now most of the verbs in this group are -go verbs, but not all of them.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now what these verbs do in the point in the past is that firstly the beginning bit of the verb, so for example if we have poder, that beginning bit, pod-, changes. And we already saw this, we saw for example they were able was pudieron, so that pod- changes to pud-. Here it's a little change, but there are more drastic changes with other verbs.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So this is the first thing: the base of the verb that is left once we take the endings off changes, sometimes radically, sometimes a little bit like here from pod- to pud-. The second thing that they do is that they use a mixture of the point endings from -ar verbs and from -er/-ir verbs. They use a mixture of the two endings from both sides, but always the same mixture for each of these irregular verbs.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And the third thing they do is to not have the accent on the endings. So firstly let's revise the point in the past with hablar and comer, just to refresh what are these endings.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we have hablar to speak, and I spoke is?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And he spoke or she spoke or you formal spoke?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Habló. And then we had to eat, which was comer, and I ate?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Comí. And he ate or she ate or you formal ate, it ate? Habló and then with comer it's?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Comió. Good. Back to hablar, how was we spoke?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Hablamos, good, same as the present tense. And they spoke?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Hablaron. And you informal spoke, which in the you informal version we hear that informal s and the informal t in the ending?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Hablaste, good. Back to comer, how is we ate?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Comimos. They ate or you guys ate?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. Comiste. So that's the panorama of our dot in the past. But these irregular verbs use a mixture of these two groups for different endings in the point in the past. For example, tener to have, in the point in the past the way that ten- changes, that root changes, we said that's the first thing that happens, the ten- of tener becomes tuv-, T-U-V.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And I had is tuve, and he, she, it had is tuvo. So we're not accenting the endings: tuve, tuvo. So where are these two endings coming from, -e and -o? Are they coming from the -ar verbs or from the -er/-ir verbs?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So we have tuve and tuvo. So these two endings for I and for he, she, it, you formal come from -ar, and the rest come from -er/-ir. So how would you say we had with the point in the past?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Tuvieron. Good. So now that we've worked our way through this one verb, all we need to do for the other ones is to find the base, the irregular base for the verb, and then we know what to do with it. What was to be for states?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Estar. Now I was, the point in the past from estar is estuve. So it's nice to look at tener and estar together, because we have tuve for I had and estuve for I was.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. He was, she was, you were formal?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: ¿Dónde estuviste? They were, you guys were?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. ¿Dónde estuvieron? So whilst we have these irregular forms, which need a little bit more effort, many times you can just use the line in the past instead. So if you say something like ¿Dónde estuviste?, where were you?, and here we're using a point in time, so maybe it sounds like where were you in this precise moment when we needed you. But even even so, we could still just use the line in the past to get around this irregular tense. Now we don't want to avoid it forever, huh? Anything that we don't control of the language will end up controlling us. Anything we are uncertain of that we don't take the control of will control us. But many times you're in a conversation and you don't have time to find that irregular form, and maybe you want to worry about it later and check and think about what it was, in that case you can just turn to the line in the past: ¿Dónde estabas? instead of ¿Dónde estuviste?.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how would you say I had to go using this point in the past? So how is I had using the point in the past?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So I had to go?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So tuve que ir you would want to use it if you meant that in one precise moment, you know, something happened and I had to go, tuve que ir. But you could also use the line in the past and not have any problem there if you wanted to avoid this irregular tense just to get the meaning across. So you can just say tenía que ir, which is regular, to avoid using this irregular tense. What was to say or to tell?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Decir or contar, but decir we are working with for now. So dec- becomes dij- in the point in the past, dij-, D-I-J. Now if we follow what we did with the other verbs we can find all of the different versions: I said, he said. So let's work our way through it. What is I said?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Dijimos, good. So they are using the same endings, this group of irregular verbs: -e and -o from the -ar group and then the rest of the endings from the -er/-ir group for the point in the past.
